text: A sermon is a performance given to an audience that cannot walk out, and the pastor at the center of Mass Appeal knows exactly how well he plays the room. Into his parish comes a seminarian with no interest in playing it at all. Glenn Jordan keeps the picture to ninety-nine minutes and mostly indoors, which is the right scale, since the whole quarrel is between two men, one of whom holds the pulpit and the other of whom wants it used differently. Neither position is safe. The older man's charm is a survival skill inside an institution that rewards the agreeable; the younger man's honesty is spent partly out of other people's pockets. The National Board of Review placed it among the ten films of its year. It works as an argument that keeps refusing to declare a winner.

Eighty-three minutes, a stretch of front line in Korea, and one man in the platoon nobody wants to look at directly. War Hunt puts an American arrival with his convictions intact next to a soldier who has found something in night patrols that he likes. The brevity is the point. There is no campaign here, only the ground between two positions and the hours after dark, and the film stays down at squad level, where the difficulty is not the enemy but the person sleeping a few feet away. Denis Sanders shot it in 1962, near enough to the war that the question was still open rather than settled. The discomfort that holds it together is practical: the army has obvious uses for such a man, and no visible plan for him once the shooting stops.

A scholarship takes Davey Fenwick out of the mining village, and a marriage brings him back before the degree is done, installed as the local schoolteacher. Carol Reed refuses to keep the two halves of that sentence apart. The dispute between the owners and the men, and the arrangement between a husband and a wife, run on the same fuel: what can be afforded, and who decides. Jenny wants a life a half-trained man can pay for. The miners want somebody lettered enough to argue their case. Davey cannot manage both, and the film is unsentimental about how small the resulting compromise looks from inside a rented house. Reed keeps the scale domestic even when the subject is a coalfield, so the anger arrives not in speeches but in the arithmetic of wages and rent.

Seven years after the riots in Watts, a concert filled a Los Angeles stadium, and Mel Stuart aimed his cameras at the stage and at the streets outside it in roughly equal measure. The cutting between them is the film. A number is allowed to run its full length, and then the picture is out among people talking about rent, work, police, church, and what the word soul is being asked to carry that year. Neither register is used to explain the other. They interrupt each other for ninety-eight minutes, and the interruptions accumulate into something no straight concert record could hold. The National Film Registry keeps a copy. What is preserved there is mostly talk, cut as tightly as the music, from a neighborhood that agreed for one afternoon to be looked at.

Someone has to decide what goes on the panel: the name, first, and then whatever else will fit. Common Threads films that decision in the weeks before the 1987 march on Washington, and reduces a memorial of thousands of names to six of them. The people sewing are widowers, mothers, friends, and Rob Epstein lets them work with their hands while they speak, which keeps the interviews from hardening into testimony. Around those rooms he sets the public record: news footage, official statements, the pace at which institutions moved while these six were ill. The Academy gave it the documentary feature award. Eighty minutes is a strict length for material this large, and the strictness is the method, a national emergency divided by six and then multiplied outward again.

It was made to be watched from a school desk, and its slogan concedes the whole situation: We Must Be Ready. Nine minutes long, mixing animation with live-action footage and a narrator's steady voice, Duck and Cover teaches children a drill to perform when a signal comes, treating the atomic bomb as a hazard that rewards preparation, like traffic or fire. The division of labor is deliberate. Drawing carries the instruction, because a cartoon can stay cheerful where a photograph cannot, and the filmed children then repeat the movements until they look like an ordinary part of the school day. What holds now is not the advice but the address: patient, unhurried, pitched at children. Anthony Rizzo directed it in 1951. The Registry has it, and the reason is audible in the narration.

School lets out, and for a few weeks a girl who spends term time on the outside of everything has a friend. Then classes resume. Yoon Ga-eun shoots The World of Us at child height, where exclusion runs through invitations, birthdays, and who was told what first, and where an adult standing two feet higher will miss most of the traffic. The film declines to treat any of this as rehearsal for adult life; it is simply the life these two are living. The hard part is that the newcomer has her own reasons to trade one loyalty for another, so the cruelty circulates rather than descending from a single source. Ninety-five minutes, no villain available, and a patience with children's faces that never turns them into illustrations.

The English title indicates a building; the French one, Goupi Mains Rouges, indicates a man and the nickname attached to his hands. That gap covers most of what matters in Jacques Becker's mystery. An old woman dies at a country inn, the suspects are her own relatives, and these people have shared ground and table long enough to have nicknames for one another. Becker cares less about which of them did it than about the household economy that made it thinkable: who farms, who is owed, who expects to inherit, who has been waiting a very long time. Much of it is funny, because the family would be exhausting to live among even with nobody dead. France, 1946, 104 minutes, an investigation conducted largely at the kitchen table.

It arrived a week at a time, and the audience came back a week at a time, which is a different contract from the one a feature signs. Pearl White plays Pauline through installments that keep putting her in physical danger and keep requiring her to work her own way out; the damsel label has clung to the serial ever since, and the surviving footage does not really support it. What survives is not the original run but nine episodes of a condensed 1916 reissue, just under seven hours, with much of the connective tissue gone. Watching it now involves a certain amount of reconstruction. Louis J. Gasnier stages for immediate legibility, the predicament readable in seconds, the escape delivered before the reel runs out, and invention has to arrive on schedule.

A conversation goes wrong on a farm in Texas in 1901, a lawman is dead, and Gregorio Cortez is on a horse with the state coming after him. What follows is a Western measured in distance: days of riding, a manhunt of a size that becomes its own subject, and a pursuit that Robert M. Young films from both sides without granting either the comfort of villainy. The Rangers are men doing a job in haste, working from an account of the event that was already unreliable when it left the farm. Cortez, meanwhile, is turning into a story while he is still riding. The ballad in the title got there first and settled everything. The film goes back to the week before the song, when nobody chasing him and nobody helping him knew what it would be called.

A small-town beauty contest promises its winner a job in pictures, and the job does not exist. Ella learns this at the studio gate, having already left a stepmother and her daughters behind her, and the 1926 comedy that follows is the movie business making jokes about the movie business at a moment when it had only recently finished building the walls she is standing outside of. Alfred E. Green runs it at seventy-five minutes and hands most of the work to his star, whose face does the arithmetic in close-up while the plot arranges another closed door. The fairy-tale scaffolding is dispatched briskly. What the film wants to watch is a girl with no money and no introductions trying to get past a gate.
